title: Kailasa at Ellora: Carved From the Top Down

segments.say: This temple was never built. It was cut out of a hillside, from the top down.

anim.title: Carved, not built
items: Start at the top of the rock
Cut away the hill around it

segments.say: Carvers started at the top of the rock and dug downward, removing the hill until only the temple was left. It is a single piece of stone, the largest monolithic temple at Ellora.
Kailasa is cave sixteen of thirty-four at Ellora, in Maharashtra. Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves sit side by side, which UNESCO reads as a sign of tolerance.
The temple is covered in sculpture. One famous panel shows Ravana trying to lift Mount Kailasa, the home of Shiva.

items.text: work generally credited to Rashtrakuta king Krishna I
later Rashtrakuta rulers add to it
Ellora becomes a World Heritage Site

segments.say: Most of the work is generally credited to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna the First, in the eighth century, though no inscription on the temple itself says so.

anim.below: from the courtyard floor to the top of the shrine

segments.say: The top of the shrine rises thirty-two point six metres above the courtyard, all of it carved from one rock.
For GS One, remember: Ellora, cave sixteen, the Rashtrakutas, and a temple carved from the top down.

sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ellora Caves (whc.unesco.org/en/list/243): 34 caves in the Charanandri hills, Maharashtra; Buddhist caves 1–12, Brahmanical caves 13–29 including Kailasa (cave 16), Jaina caves 30–34; Cave 16 the largest monolithic temple; Ravana lifting Mount Kailasa panel; spirit of tolerance; uninterrupted sequence AD 600–1000; inscribed 1983

Wikipedia, 'Kailasa temple, Ellora' (read): vertical excavation, carvers started at the top of the rock and excavated downward; no dedicatory inscription; generally attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I (8th century), attribution not completely certain; later Rashtrakuta rulers may have extended it; top of the structure over the sanctuary 32.6 m above the court

quiz.q: Which dynasty is the Kailasa temple at Ellora generally credited to?
quiz.why: Generally attributed to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I.

quiz.q: Which cave number is the Kailasa temple?
quiz.why: UNESCO: Kailasa is cave 16, in the Brahmanical group (13–29).

quiz.q: Ellora's caves belong to which traditions?

reviewNote: Site facts are from UNESCO; the construction method, the Krishna I attribution and the 32.6 m height are from Wikipedia (the attribution is itself hedged there, and the script keeps the hedge). Check against ASI's Ellora page before approval. UNESCO calls Kailasa 'the largest monolithic temple' without saying 'at Ellora'; the script says 'at Ellora' to stay safe. Moving facts: none.
